title: I took my AI-assisted game to a physical indie game expo — and people actually enjoyed it
author: I-want-to-say
selftext:
https://preview.redd.it/gw7pfpvunirh1.png?width=1422&format=png&auto=webp&s=0d40cc7e250b1e00874180bb27b67cee47d22fad

I was a bit nervous about how people would react to my game. With all the negativity surrounding AI-generated and AI-assisted games online, I really wasn’t sure what to expect.

To my surprise, the response at the expo was very positive.

The game attracted quite a lot of attention, especially from people in their 30s and 40s, but also from kids. What surprised me even more was that the expo lasted two days, and quite a few players actually came back the next day just to play another round.

The wishlist numbers weren’t huge, but that wasn’t really the most important part for me. Seeing people stop, play, laugh and come back gave me a lot more confidence in continuing the project.

It was also an interesting reminder that the conversation around AI games online can feel very different from how regular players react when they simply sit down and play the game.

replies.author: Maple-Syrup89
replies.body:
While we are ranting, I totally agree there are amazing AI assisted games, and before there was AI, there was plenty of what I have been calling "human slop." I try to push back against the anti-ai folks and argue it is about quality and care, not the tool you use. 

As a woodworker I know exactly zero customers will care if I used a $16,000 automated table saw or a $40 skil saw or a $5 rusty hand saw, when making their table. It is about the result. I could kill my arms and take 10x as long to cut with the hand saw, insisting it is artisanal, but dang, thats not a good way to work and people will pay for the result, and the economy of it. 

If I use only hand tools and charge 8k for a table because of how much time it took, my customer base is essentially nobody. If I make the same table for $1k, and I can make 10 of them in less time, now I am cooking. 

I find people have had a really hard time truly understanding what we have here.

comments.author: YoungXardas
comments.body: Are those assets used in your game also AI-generated? If so, can you share your workflow? What did you use? Those pixel arts look so consistent.

replies.author: I-want-to-say
replies.body:
Thanks! My workflow is actually quite complex. The main priority is consistency — it’s still not always perfect, but that’s where the number of iterations and the amount of tools I use really matter.

I usually start with GPT Image -> Runway ->Autosprite -> Claude and Grok for coding — all paid versions. If one tool doesn’t give me what I need, I move to another one. The process is very iterative, and I rarely (if at all) get a final asset from a single generation.

Most assets still require manual polishing: removing stray pixels, fixing gaps or “holes”, adjusting colors, cleaning outlines, etc. AI still makes plenty of small mistakes in pixel art.

I’d say my pipeline still very much resembles regular game development — just without the requirement of having a several-person team. There’s still a lot of iteration, testing, fixing and manual polishing involved.

comments.author: fraxis
comments.body: Great job!  Wishlisted.  Can you tell us about your AI behind the scenes?  Claude/GOT?  Unity or Godot or ? (and the reason you picked the engine you did).  How many hours do you have into it so far?  What guidance/suggestions can you give to other aspiring AI game creators who want to use AI not only to create but also to distribute through Steam?   Thanks.

replies.author: I-want-to-say
replies.body:
Thanks! It’s made in Godot.

The project actually started as a 12-hour experiment where I wanted to see how far I could get mostly through prompting. Back then I used Moonlake AI a lot, and now my workflow is a mix of Claude Code, Grok, Runway, GPT Image, Autosprite, Suno and manual work.

I stopped counting hours a long time ago tbh😅 As I said - the first playable version took around 12 hours, but I’ve been working on the game in my spare time for about six months now.

As for advice: start small. Don’t try to make your dream game as your first AI-assisted project. Make something simple, get the core loop working, and learn how the tools behave.

Also, the more specific you are, the better the results. Give examples, explain what you want, what you don’t want, and keep iterating. AI is fast, but it still needs a lot of direction. all those " I made a game with one prompt" posts are either fake or do not tell the truth. You can get working prototype in one prompt but it will be very basic,. To have a game that is actually fun to play you need to spend hours or days on iterations.

And for Steam specifically, I’d treat it like any other game. Make sure it’s fun, stable, and polished enough that people want to keep playing it.
